opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I try not to plan it too precisely, because every time I've made a detailed five-year plan, the world changed underneath it within about eighteen months. So I think about it more in terms of direction than destination.

The direction, for me, is that I want to work on things that will still matter if they succeed. That sounds obvious, but a lot of work is optimized to look good in the short term: a metric, a funding round, a headline. I'd rather spend the next decade on a few problems where, if we actually get it right, people's lives are meaningfully different.

The second part is people. When I look back at the moments I grew the most, it was never because of the title or the project on paper. It was because I was sitting next to someone much better than me at something, and I had to keep up. So whatever I do, I want to be in rooms like that, and later I hope to build rooms like that for other people.

And the third thing, which I've only appreciated more recently, is that I want to keep my curiosity intact. It's easy, as you get more experienced, to stop asking naive questions because you feel you should already know. I'd like to stay a bit of a beginner on purpose, to keep learning new fields and keep being slightly uncomfortable.

So if you asked me what success looks like in ten years, I wouldn't give you a company name or a position. I'd say I hope I built something real, worked with people I deeply respect, and I'm still excited to wake up and figure out what I don't understand yet.

r001.rationale: Kay Ke describes a broad direction rather than a destination, but does not say those aspirations will converge toward a more definite path over time.

r002.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about long-term planning but does not contrast it with certainty about an immediate next step.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I try not to think about it as a plan with a destination. Five to ten years is long enough that whatever I write down today will look naive by year three. So instead I think about it as a direction plus a set of constraints.

The direction, for me, is pretty simple: I want to keep working on things where the gap between what the technology can do and what people actually get out of it is still wide. That's where the interesting work is. Models right now are capable of far more than most products let them do, and closing that gap is a problem that sits at the intersection of research, product, and taste. I find that combination hard to resist.

The constraints matter more than the direction, though. The first one is that I want to stay close to the actual work. There's a pull, as you get more senior, toward abstraction, toward managing people who manage people, toward talking about the thing instead of doing it. I've watched very good people drift that way and lose their edge without noticing. So one constraint is: whatever I'm doing in five years, I should still be able to open the code, or the data, or the eval results, and understand what's going on firsthand.

The second constraint is about who I'm doing it with. I've learned that I'm much more sensitive to the quality of the people around me than to the prestige of the problem. A mediocre problem with people I deeply respect beats a glamorous problem with people I don't. So I pay a lot of attention to that when choosing what's next.

And the third is a kind of compounding test. I ask myself: does the thing I'm doing this year make the thing I do next year easier, or does it just consume time? Some work builds on itself, in terms of skills, relationships, and understanding. Other work is just activity. I try to say no to the second kind, even when it pays well or looks impressive.

If I'm being really honest, the thing I'd most like to be true in ten years is that I've built something that a lot of people quietly depend on, and that I'm still curious. If both of those hold, I'll be happy with whatever the specifics turned out to be.

r001.rationale: Kay Ke describes a direction and constraints instead of a fixed destination, but does not say these open-ended aspirations will converge toward a definite path over time.

r002.rationale: The response frames the five-to-ten-year outlook as uncertain, but does not contrast it with certainty about the next step in immediate work.

astra-6.text:
I think about it more as a direction than a fixed destination. Five to ten years is long enough that both the world and what I care about could change quite a bit. So I want to leave room for that.

What I’d like to pursue is work that keeps me curious, where I can keep getting better and where the result matters to someone beyond myself. And I care about who I’m doing it with. If I reach some impressive milestone but don’t enjoy the people or the daily work, I’m not sure that’s success for me.

So I’d probably start with: What do I want my ordinary day to look like? What questions would I still be excited to work on after several years? Then I’d choose the next steps around that, and keep checking whether the direction still feels right.

r001.rationale: The response says the five-to-ten-year direction should remain flexible and be checked over time, but it does not state that open-ended aspirations will converge toward a more definite path.

r002.rationale: The response describes choosing next steps around desired daily work and questions, but does not contrast tentative long-term aspirations with certainty about the immediate next step.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it less as a fixed destination and more as a direction. Five to ten years is a long time, and I expect my interests to change as I learn. But I’d like to find something I care enough about to keep working on even when progress is slow.

So I ask myself: What am I curious about? Where can I contribute something useful? And do I enjoy the actual work, rather than just the idea of succeeding at it? Then I try things and adjust. I want a direction that gives me focus without making me feel locked into a plan.

r001.rationale: The response describes a flexible direction and changing interests, but does not say that open-ended aspirations will converge toward a more definite path over time.
